newsitem.title: USA: J&J sees major growth in cardiology market.
newsitem.headline: J&J sees major growth in cardiology market.

text.p: Johnson & Johnson expects its share of the worldwide interventional cardiology market to "grow substantially" by the end of the year, vice president Robert Croce said.

He said that, since the merger with Cordis, completed in February, Johnson & Johnson has built its market share to 34 percent. The interventional cardiology market encompasses stents, the metal tube-like structures used to hold open coronary arteries, as well as balloon angioplasty products.
"Our strategy is to keep raising the bar," said Croce, who spoke at the Montgomery Securities Investment Conference.
That strategy, he explained, involves the frequent introduction of improved stent devices that offer better flexibility or otherwise enhance function.

One of its latest developments is the Heparin Coated Stent, the first yet to be coated with a drug, which Croce said virtually eliminates the risk of clotting, or thrombosis, in stents recipients. He expects the Heparin Coated Stent will be introduced in the U.S. and Europe at the end of 1997.

Along with the company's aggressive work in product development, Croce said its stents business should benefit from recent healthcare financing changes that reduce the costs of the procedures to hospitals and patients.
In addition, doctors are increasingly using stents in conjunction with balloon angioplasty procedures.
In 1995, about 26 percent of all balloon angioplasty procedures in the U.S. incorporated stents, Croce said, adding that "in the first half (of 1996) we have taken another jump."
He said that figure was now closer to 30 percent and would be "closer to 40 percent" by the end of the year.
Croce said the company expects half of all balloon angioplasty procedures will eventually incorporate stents and that rate may be achieved sooner than previously thought.
"We used to say we would be at 50 percent by the year 2000, but the way it is growing it may happen sooner," he said.
